title: Complexity
summary: Bound time and space in big-O, including amortized cost.

parts.rule: Estimate how running time and memory scale as the input length n increases. Keep the leading term and discard fixed multipliers. Two nested loops that each run about n times are quadratic unless the inner range shrinks. Halving the remaining span each step is logarithmic. A recursion that splits into two full-size branches without sharing work is exponential. Include output size and call-stack depth in the space story. When a rare expensive step is paid for by many cheap ones, label the average as amortized.
parts.why: Almost every non-trivial board question ends with "and the complexity?" People miscount loops, mix amortized append with the cost of one resizing append, or omit stack depth. Giving a tight bound plus the amortized caveat reads as deliberate engineering judgment.
parts.example: Snippet A touches every cell of an n by n grid with a double loop: about n² touches, O(n²) time, and no extra arrays beyond the input. Snippet B sets i = n and repeatedly replaces i with i//2 until it hits zero: roughly log₂ n steps, O(log n). Snippet C appends into a dynamic buffer that doubles when full. A single resizing append copies the old contents (worst-case linear), yet growing from length 1 to n copies fewer than 2n elements overall, so a long series of appends is amortized constant per append. At n = 10⁵, an n log n approach is near 1.7 million operations; an n² approach is near ten billion and usually misses a one-second budget. Say whether the interviewer wanted the worst single call or the amortized sequence.
parts.use: Reach for big-O when you compare two designs before writing code. Use amortized wording for doubling vectors, some tree rebalancing schemes, and union-find. State time and space separately whenever recursion depth or output size is large.
parts.refuse: Do not drop the leading term to make the answer sound friendlier. Do not call a true double-n loop "basically linear." Do not quote amortized constant time when the question asked for the worst cost of one operation. Do not leave recursion depth out of the space bound.

body:
Rule. Estimate how running time and memory scale as the input length n increases. Keep the leading term and discard fixed multipliers. Two nested loops that each run about n times are quadratic unless the inner range shrinks. Halving the remaining span each step is logarithmic. A recursion that splits into two full-size branches without sharing work is exponential. Include output size and call-stack depth in the space story. When a rare expensive step is paid for by many cheap ones, label the average as amortized.

Why it matters. Almost every non-trivial board question ends with "and the complexity?" People miscount loops, mix amortized append with the cost of one resizing append, or omit stack depth. Giving a tight bound plus the amortized caveat reads as deliberate engineering judgment.

Worked example. Snippet A touches every cell of an n by n grid with a double loop: about n² touches, O(n²) time, and no extra arrays beyond the input. Snippet B sets i = n and repeatedly replaces i with i//2 until it hits zero: roughly log₂ n steps, O(log n). Snippet C appends into a dynamic buffer that doubles when full. A single resizing append copies the old contents (worst-case linear), yet growing from length 1 to n copies fewer than 2n elements overall, so a long series of appends is amortized constant per append. At n = 10⁵, an n log n approach is near 1.7 million operations; an n² approach is near ten billion and usually misses a one-second budget. Say whether the interviewer wanted the worst single call or the amortized sequence.

[[diagram:growth]]

[[diagram:growth-png]]

When to use. Reach for big-O when you compare two designs before writing code. Use amortized wording for doubling vectors, some tree rebalancing schemes, and union-find. State time and space separately whenever recursion depth or output size is large.

When to refuse. Do not drop the leading term to make the answer sound friendlier. Do not call a true double-n loop "basically linear." Do not quote amortized constant time when the question asked for the worst cost of one operation. Do not leave recursion depth out of the space bound.
